question: Tell me about a time a project’s scope, requirements, or priorities changed significantly midstream. How did you adjust?

raiseTranscript.text: I was building a reporting dashboard for our ops team. Two weeks in, leadership shifted priority to mobile-first because field agents needed it on tablets. I paused, listed the new must-haves, cut two desktop-only charts, and asked my mentor for a quick review of the revised plan.
Delivered the mobile version on the original date. The ops manager said it cut their field reporting time by half. I learned to surface trade-offs early instead of trying to do everything.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time a project’s scope, requirements, or priorities changed significantly midstream. How did you adjust?
Role: New grad on first dashboard project
Situation: Ops dashboard, midstream shift to mobile-first for field agents
Actions: Listed new must-haves, cut two desktop charts, asked mentor for plan review
Outcome: Hit original date; ops manager noted halved field reporting time
Quote: "I learned to surface trade-offs early instead of trying to do everything."
Follow-up: What was the outcome? - Hit date, positive feedback, clear learning point
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at junior level. Candidate described a clear scope change on their first project and responded by reprioritizing work and seeking quick input rather than pushing back. Quote shows they internalized the need to surface trade-offs. This demonstrates coachability and ownership of their own deliverables without overclaiming impact. Biggest strength is the explicit link between the change and the adjustment they made.

lowerTranscript.text: The PM added three new features halfway through. I kept working on the original list because I thought the new stuff would slip the date. Ended up delivering late and the team had to cut the new items anyway.
Did you talk to anyone about the change?
I mentioned it in standup but no one really helped so I just kept going.

Story shows passive response to a common early-career situation. The outcome was predictable slippage with no evidence of learning or ownership. Biggest gap is absence of any proactive adjustment or request for guidance.

raiseTranscript.text: We were building a shared billing service for two teams. Mid-sprint, finance changed the revenue recognition rules, forcing a data-model rewrite. I pulled the two tech leads together, mapped the new requirements, and proposed we split the work so each team owned their integration points.
How did the other teams respond?
One lead pushed back on the split. I walked through the timeline impact and we landed on a phased rollout instead. We shipped the core change in four weeks with both teams unblocked.

senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at senior level. Candidate drove a cross-team response to an external priority shift by convening leads and negotiating a workable split. Quote illustrates influence without authority and focus on unblocking others. Impact stayed scoped to the service but shows clear coordination beyond their own code. Biggest strength is the proactive stakeholder alignment that prevented broader delay.

I sent them the updated spec and moved on. They eventually figured it out.

raiseTranscript.text: My team was three sprints into a platform migration when product reprioritized toward a new compliance deadline. I reset the roadmap with the team, identified two engineers to pair on the compliance work, and reallocated the rest to keep the migration moving in parallel.
How did you handle the engineers whose work was deprioritized?
I met with each one, explained the business reason, and gave them clear ownership of pieces of the compliance track so they still had visible impact.

Biggest strength is the combination of roadmap reset and attention to team members whose work was disrupted.

raiseTranscript.text: Six months into a multi-year infrastructure program, regulatory changes in two regions forced us to redesign the data residency architecture. I convened the regional leads and product VPs, ran a two-week option analysis, and recommended we split the program into a core platform plus region-specific extensions to preserve the original global timeline.
What trade-offs did you surface to the board?
We accepted a 15% budget increase in year one to avoid a nine-month delay. The board approved after I showed the revenue at risk if we missed the regulatory dates.
